From "if it rains, the ground is wet" you can build three relatives by swapping and negating:
"if the ground is wet, it rained" (converse), "if it does not rain, the ground is not wet" (inverse),

thing as the original: if the ground is dry, it cannot have rained, because rain would have made it
wet. The converse is a different claim (a sprinkler can wet the ground).
The converse and the inverse are contrapositives of each other, so they are equivalent to each other.

In propositional logic, a truth table settles every question: list the rows, read the column. A
first-order formula has no such table. Its truth depends on a whole

: which objects exist,
and which predicates hold of which objects. There are infinitely many possible worlds, of every size.
So the questions change shape. "Is this formula always true?" becomes "is it true in

world?",
and the usual way to answer "no" is to

This lesson is about that skill, plus the short list of quantifier laws that let you rewrite formulas
safely. Half of them are two-way equivalences; the other half work in

, and GATE
asks about exactly that difference again and again ("which of these is valid?", "which is NOT
equivalent?"). For each one-way law we keep a two-element counter-model in our pocket.

The lesson runs in four parts: what a world is and what "valid" means; the laws, with a proof for each
valid direction and a counter-model for each invalid one; moving quantifiers past formulas that do not
mention their variable, which leads to prenex form; and a gallery of sentences whose models are
special (always true, only infinite, always small). Every GATE question on the topic sits in one of
these four parts, and each part ends with worked examples taken from them.

gave quantifiers their meaning and taught translation and
negation. Here we treat formulas as objects to be classified: valid, satisfiable or unsatisfiable,
exactly as

classified propositional formulas as
tautologies, contingencies and contradictions. The counter-model habit is reused in every later
chapter: a relation that is "almost" transitive, a group table that is "almost" associative, a graph
that "should" be Hamiltonian. The last sections touch the edge of what logic can decide, which
returns in Theory of Computation as undecidability.

set.text: counterexample for both: p = F, q = T

falsify-tree.title: The falsification test
falsify-tree.intro: To test ((a → b) ∧ (b → c)) → (a → c), assume it is false and follow the forced values until they clash or settle.

elements.text: Trying to falsify the hypothetical syllogism

elements.label: so a = T and c = F
so a→b = T and b→c = T
a = T and a → b = T force b = T
b = T and b → c = T force c = T
clash: c = T and c = F

steps.caption: Assume the whole implication is F. An implication is false only as T → F, so the hypothesis must be T and the conclusion F.
The conclusion a → c is F, which forces a = T and c = F. These values are now fixed.
The hypothesis is a true conjunction, so both parts are T: a → b = T and b → c = T.
a is T and a → b is T, so b must be T (otherwise a → b would be T → F).
b is T and b → c is T, so c must be T. But c was already forced to F.
A clash: no row can make the formula false, so it is a tautology. No branching was needed; every value was forced.

forall-big-and.title: ∀ is a big AND
forall-big-and.intro: The domain has four elements. P is true at a, b and d, and false at c. Watch the universal check every element.

elements.text: ∀x P(x) on the domain {a, b, c, d}: one big AND

steps.caption: A universal claim has one term per element. On a four-element domain, ∀x P(x) is the conjunction P(a) ∧ P(b) ∧ P(c) ∧ P(d).
Check a: P(a) is true. The claim survives this element.
Check b: P(b) is true. Still no counterexample.
Check c: P(c) is false. One false term makes the whole AND false: c is a counterexample.
d is true as well, but it no longer matters: a universal needs every element, and c already failed.
So ∀x P(x) = T ∧ T ∧ F ∧ T = F. To refute a ∀, one counterexample is enough.

forall-exists-grid.title: The order of ∀ and ∃
forall-exists-grid.intro: A relation R on {a, b, c, d}. Read ∀x∃y along the rows and ∃y∀x down the columns.

steps.caption: R(x, y) as a grid: row x, column y, T where x is related to y. Each x is related to exactly one y here.
∀x ∃y R(x, y) asks: does every ROW contain a T? Row a has T at b, row b at c, row c at d, row d at a.
Every row has a T, so ∀x ∃y R(x, y) is true. The witness y is different for each x, and that is allowed.

set.text: ∀x∃y R: every row has a T  ✓

steps.caption: ∃y ∀x R(x, y) asks for one COLUMN that is T all the way down. Each column has an F somewhere.
No full column, so ∃y ∀x R(x, y) is false. Swapping ∀ and ∃ changed the answer.
Now make column c all T. Then ∃y ∀x R(x, y) is true (y = c works for everyone)…
…and every row automatically contains that T in column c, so ∀x ∃y R(x, y) is true too. ∃∀ implies ∀∃, never the other way.

forall-or-counter.title: Why ∀x (P ∨ Q) does not give ∀x P ∨ ∀x Q
forall-or-counter.intro: The turn-taking world: P holds at 1, Q at 2. Each element is covered, but neither predicate covers everything.

elements.text: ∀ over ∨ fails: P and Q take turns

steps.caption: A world with two elements: P is true only at 1, Q only at 2.
Element 1 is P, element 2 is Q: every element is P or Q, so ∀x (P ∨ Q) is true.
But element 2 is not P, so ∀x P is false.
And element 1 is not Q, so ∀x Q is false.
So ∀x P ∨ ∀x Q is false: ∀ does not distribute over ∨. Only the direction ∀P ∨ ∀Q → ∀(P ∨ Q) is valid.

horn-chain.title: A logic program as a first-order sentence
horn-chain.intro: One Horn rule and three facts. The rule fires once for each x that has some suitable y.

elements.text: A(x) ← B(x, y), C(y): from facts to conclusions

steps.caption: The rule says: for all x and y, if B(x, y) and C(y) then A(x). The facts are B(a, b), B(c, b) and C(b).
Match x = a, y = b: B(a, b) and C(b) both hold, so the rule fires: A(a).
Match x = c, y = b: B(c, b) and C(b) hold: A(c). Only one y is needed each time, so y is really ‘some y’.

set.text: y appears only in the body: it is ∃y

steps.caption: As a sentence: ∀x (∃y (B(x, y) ∧ C(y)) → A(x)), and the headless rule ← B(x, x) adds ∧ ¬∃x B(x, x). No fact B(x, x) exists here, so the program holds.

implication-promise.title: Implication as a promise
implication-promise.intro: An implication is a promise. It is broken only if the condition happens and the promised result does not.

elements.text: The promise “if you score above 90 (p), you get a prize (q)”

elements.label: T T: scored > 90, got the prize
F T: scored ≤ 90, got a prize

elements.text: p → q is false on one row only

steps.caption: Case T, T: you scored above 90 and got the prize. The promise was kept, so p → q is true.
Case T, F: you scored above 90 and got no prize. This is the one way to break the promise: p → q is false.
Case F, T: you scored 90 or less but got a prize anyway (maybe for something else). The promise said nothing about this case, so it is not broken: true.
Case F, F: you scored 90 or less and got nothing. Again the promise was never tested: true. A false hypothesis makes the implication vacuously true.
So p → q is false exactly when p is true and q is false; that is the same column as ¬p ∨ q.

set.text: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q (false only on T, F)

implication-square.title: Converse, inverse and contrapositive
implication-square.intro: From one implication we can build three others by swapping and negating its two sides. Only one of them says the same thing.

elements.text: The four relatives of an implication

steps.caption: Start from p → q. Swapping the sides gives the converse q → p; negating both sides gives the inverse ¬p → ¬q.
Doing both (swap and negate) gives the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p.
Test the row p = T, q = F. Original: T → F = F. Contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p = T → F = F. They fail together.
On the same row the converse is F → T = T and the inverse is F → T = T: they differ from the original, so they are not equivalent to it.
The diagonals pair up: original ≡ contrapositive, and converse ≡ inverse (each is the other's contrapositive).

infinite-chain.title: A sentence with only infinite models
infinite-chain.intro: R has successors everywhere, is transitive, asymmetric and irreflexive. Watch what happens when we try to finish a finite model.

elements.text: Every element needs a successor, and you can never come back

steps.caption: Start anywhere: d0. The first condition says it has a successor, d0 R d1.
d1 needs a successor too: d2. Transitivity adds d0 R d2 behind the scenes.
And d3. Every new element is related to all the earlier ones.
Try to stop: let d3's successor be an old element, d0. That closes a cycle d0 R d1 R d2 R d3 R d0.

set.text: d3 R d0 would close a cycle…

steps.caption: Transitivity around the cycle gives d0 R d0, which irreflexivity forbids. So no old element can be a successor.
So the chain must keep growing with new elements: no finite model exists. (ℕ, <) is a model: 0 < 1 < 2 < … forever.

knights-grid.title: Truth-tellers, liars and a coin
knights-grid.intro: A speaker's statement is true exactly when the speaker is truthful. Tabulate type against coin and keep the worlds where that rule holds.

elements.text: “Head if and only if I am telling the truth” (GATE 2015)
t: the speaker is truthful   h: the coin shows head

steps.caption: List the four possible worlds: the speaker's type times the coin. In each, evaluate the statement h ↔ t.
A truthful speaker's statement must be T and a liar's must be F. Keep a world only if the statement's value matches the type.
Two worlds survive, rows 1 and 3: (truthful, head) and (liar, head). The coin is head in both.
So the result is head, whatever the type; the type itself stays unknown. Algebraically t ↔ (h ↔ t) ≡ h.

set.text: t ↔ (h ↔ t) ≡ h: the coin is head

law-ladder.title: A ladder of laws
law-ladder.intro: Proving an equivalence by laws: one rung per law, arrows out first, then negations in, then tidy up.

elements.text: A rewrite ladder: GATE 2021's consequent becomes its antecedent

steps.caption: Rung 1: remove the outer arrow with A → B ≡ ¬A ∨ B, taking A = P ∧ Q. Always remove arrows first.
Rung 2: implication again. The formula becomes ¬(P ∧ Q) ∨ ¬Q ∨ R.
Rung 3: push the negation inward with De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) becomes ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Now every ¬ sits on a variable.
Rung 4: idempotent: ¬Q ∨ ¬Q ≡ ¬Q. The formula becomes ¬P ∨ ¬Q ∨ R.
Rung 5: ¬P ∨ ¬Q ∨ R is exactly ¬(P ∧ Q) ∨ R, i.e. (P ∧ Q) → R: the antecedent of S. So S has the shape X → X, a tautology.

set.text: antecedent ≡ consequent, so S ≡ X → X ≡ T

law-map.title: Which way do the laws go?
law-map.intro: Each pair is checked: valid left-to-right, and is the converse valid too?

elements.text: The quantifier laws: two-way and one-way

steps.caption: Six statements on the left, six on the right. For each pair we ask: does the left imply the right, and does the right imply the left?
∀ distributes over ∧: both directions hold (two-way).
∃ distributes over ∨: both directions hold (two-way).
∀P ∨ ∀Q gives ∀(P ∨ Q), but not back: the turn-taking world refutes the converse.
∃(P ∧ Q) gives ∃P ∧ ∃Q, but not back: two witnesses are not one.
∀(P → Q) gives ∀P → ∀Q, but not back: make P fail somewhere, then the right side is vacuous.
∃y∀x gives ∀x∃y, but not back: Lesson 1's grid.
Two-headed arrows are equivalences; one-headed arrows are the one-way laws GATE asks about. Learn the one-way ones with their counter-models.

model-search.title: Finding a counter-model
model-search.intro: A validity question can be refuted by one world. Here the search runs through the worlds on {1, 2} in order until the formula fails.

elements.text: Searching every world on {1, 2} for a counter-model

steps.caption: Formula: ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)) → (∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x)). With two elements, P and Q each have 4 possible extensions: 16 worlds. We try them in order.
World P = ∅, Q = ∅: the hypothesis is F, the conclusion F, so the implication is T. Not a counter-model; next world.
World P = ∅, Q = {1}: the hypothesis is F, the conclusion F, so the implication is T. Not a counter-model; next world.
World P = ∅, Q = {2}: the hypothesis is F, the conclusion F, so the implication is T. Not a counter-model; next world.
World P = ∅, Q = {1, 2}: the hypothesis is T, the conclusion T, so the implication is T. Not a counter-model; next world.
World P = {1}, Q = ∅: the hypothesis is F, the conclusion F, so the implication is T. Not a counter-model; next world.
World P = {1}, Q = {1}: the hypothesis is F, the conclusion F, so the implication is T. Not a counter-model; next world.
World P = {1}, Q = {2}: the hypothesis is T, the conclusion F, so the implication is F. A counter-model: the search stops.
One counter-model is enough to show the formula is not valid. Note the shape: P and Q take turns, so ‘each element is P or Q’ is true while neither holds everywhere.

set.text: P and Q take turns: the classic counter-model

negation-ladder.title: Negating a nested formula
negation-ladder.intro: De Morgan's laws for quantifiers, applied one symbol at a time, then the Chapter 1 law for ¬(A → B).

elements.text: Pushing ¬ inward, one symbol at a time

steps.caption: Start: the negation of “for every x there is a y with P(x) → Q(x, y)”. The ¬ sits outside both quantifiers.
Move ¬ past ∀x: it becomes ∃x and the ¬ moves inside. The variable x stays where it is.
Move ¬ past ∃y: it becomes ∀y. The order x, y is unchanged; only the kinds flipped.
Now ¬ meets an implication. A promise is broken exactly when the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails: ¬(A → B) = A ∧ ¬B.
Final form: some x has P, and every y fails Q(x, y). Check: two quantifiers flipped, the arrow became ∧, one new ¬ on Q.

set.text: same order x, y · kinds flipped · → became ∧

parse-tree.title: Reading a formula as a tree
parse-tree.intro: Precedence turns a string of symbols into a tree. The connective applied last is the root; evaluation runs from the leaves up.

elements.text: The parse tree of ¬p ∨ q ∧ r → p ↔ q
Parse tree of ¬p ∨ q ∧ r → p ↔ q
the root is the main connective

steps.caption: Precedence decides the shape: ¬ binds first, then ∧, then ∨, then →, and ↔ is applied last. So ↔ is the root (the main connective): the formula is a biconditional.
Evaluate at p = F, q = T, r = F. Start at the leaves: write each variable's value.
Lowest operators next: ¬p = T, and q ∧ r = T ∧ F = F.
One level up: ¬p ∨ (q ∧ r) = T ∨ F = T.
The implication has hypothesis T and conclusion p = F: T → F = F, its one false row.
The root compares its two sides: F ↔ T = F, because they disagree. A truth table is this tree evaluated once per row.

set.text: value at p = F, q = T, r = F: F

prenex-steps.title: Converting to prenex form
prenex-steps.intro: Rename bound variables apart, then pull quantifiers out, flipping those that leave a hypothesis.

elements.text: Prenex form, one move at a time

steps.caption: Start: an implication whose two sides are quantified, both with the letter x.
Rename bound variables apart.
∀x leaves the hypothesis: flips to ∃x.
∃y leaves the conclusion: unchanged.
All quantifiers are now in front: the prefix ∃x ∃y says this is an ∃∃ sentence, so it has a model iff it has one with at most 2 elements.

pull-past-w.title: A quantifier leaving a hypothesis flips
pull-past-w.intro: W does not mention x. Compare ∀x (p(x) → W) with ∃x p(x) → W and with the tempting ∀x p(x) → W.

elements.text: Pulling ∀x out of a hypothesis flips it: ∀x (p(x) → W) ≡ ∃x p(x) → W
Domain {1, 2}; p true at 1 only; W has no x

steps.caption: W is a sentence without x, so it is simply T or F. We compare three formulas in both cases.
∀x (p(x) → W): if W is T every promise is kept; if W is F the promise fails at x = 1 (p is true there).
∃x p(x) → W gives the same column: someone (1) is p, so it equals W.
∀x p(x) → W differs when W is F: ∀x p is false (2 is not p), so the implication is vacuously true.

set.text: ∀x p → W is NOT the same (GATE 2020)

steps.caption: Why: p(x) → W is ¬p(x) ∨ W. Pulling ∀x past W gives ∀x ¬p(x) ∨ W = ¬∃x p(x) ∨ W = ∃x p(x) → W. The hidden ¬ flips ∀ to ∃.

set.text: a hypothesis hides a ¬, and ¬ flips the quantifier

resolution-tree.title: A resolution tree
resolution-tree.intro: Resolution proves a conclusion by adding its negation and cancelling complementary literals until the empty clause appears.

elements.text: Resolution refutation: proving r from p ∨ q, p → r, q → r

steps.caption: Write the premises as clauses (p → r is ¬p ∨ r, q → r is ¬q ∨ r) and add the negation of the goal, ¬r. If this set is unsatisfiable, r follows.
Resolve ¬p ∨ r with ¬r on the pair r, ¬r: the resolvent is ¬p.
Resolve ¬q ∨ r with ¬r in the same way: the resolvent is ¬q.
Resolve p ∨ q with ¬p on the pair p, ¬p: the resolvent is q.
Resolve q with ¬q: nothing is left. The empty clause □ is false in every world, so the clause set is unsatisfiable and r follows.

set.text: □ derived: {p ∨ q, p → r, q → r} ⊨ r

rule-chain.title: Contrapositive, then chain
rule-chain.intro: Two implications that do not line up can often be chained after taking a contrapositive.

elements.text: c: known corrupt   e: elected   k: kind

steps.caption: Translate both sentences about one candidate: S1 is c → ¬e and S2 is k → e. The middle letters do not match: one says ¬e, the other e.
Take the contrapositive of S1: c → ¬e is equivalent to e → ¬c. Now e appears as a hypothesis.
S2 ends in e and the rewritten S1 starts with e. Hypothetical syllogism chains them: k → e and e → ¬c give k → ¬c.
k → ¬c is option C: if a person is kind, he is not known to be corrupt. Options A, B and D each have a row with S1 and S2 true and the option false.

scope-bracket.title: Scope, bound and free
scope-bracket.intro: Each quantifier owns its variable inside its scope. An occurrence outside every scope is free.

elements.text: Who owns which variable? ∀x (P(x) → ∃y R(x, y)) ∧ Q(x)

steps.caption: A quantifier binds as tightly as ¬: ∀x applies to the next unit, which here is the whole bracket ( … ).

set.text: scope of ∀x: the bracket after it

steps.caption: Inside that bracket, ∃y owns the y in R(x, y). Its scope is just R(x, y).
The x in P(x) and in R(x, y) are inside the scope of ∀x: they are bound.

set.text: bound: x in P(x), x and y in R(x, y)

steps.caption: The bracket closes before ∧. The x in Q(x) is outside every quantifier on x: it is free.

set.text: the x in Q(x) is free

steps.caption: A formula with a free variable is not a sentence: its value depends on what x is. To cover Q(x) too, bracket the whole conjunction after ∀x.

small-model.title: The small-model property
small-model.intro: Universal claims survive when elements are removed; existential witnesses must stay. Keep only the witnesses.

steps.caption: A model of φ with 7 elements. The sentence starts with three ∃'s, then only ∀'s, and has no function symbols.
Pick the witnesses for s, t and u, say elements 1, 2 and 3.
Send the other four elements away, and keep the predicates as they were on 1, 2, 3.
The witnesses are still here, and every ∀ now ranges over fewer elements, each instance with the same value as before. So φ is still true.

set.text: a model with at most 3 elements

steps.caption: So if φ has any model, it has one of size ≤ 3 (GATE 2018, option A). Nothing forces a model to be large or exactly 7.

some-are-wrong.title: Some A are B: ∧ not →
some-are-wrong.intro: Domain: a dog that does not bark, and a cat. A(x): x is a dog. B(x): x barks.

elements.text: “Some dog barks”: ∃x (A ∧ B) versus the wrong ∃x (A → B)

steps.caption: A world with one silent dog and a cat. The English sentence is false here: no dog barks.
Column A ∧ B: the dog does not bark, and the cat is not a dog. No row is T.
So ∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x)) is false, matching the sentence.
Column A → B: the dog breaks the promise (T → F), but the cat keeps it vacuously (F → F = T).
One T row is enough for ∃, so ∃x (A(x) → B(x)) is true, witnessed by the cat. It says the opposite of the sentence.
Rule: an existential over a noun takes ∧. With →, any object outside the noun is a free witness.

translate-steps.title: English to logic, phrase by phrase
translate-steps.intro: “There is a person who does not know anyone else, but that person is known by everyone else.”

elements.label: and y does not know x

steps.caption: “There is a person” fixes one y first, before anyone else is considered: the outer quantifier is ∃y.
“everyone else” ranges over every x other than y: a universal restricted by x ≠ y, so it takes →.
“is known by everyone else”: each such x knows y, M(x, y).
“does not know anyone else”: y does not know x, joined with ∧ inside the same promise.
Assembled: ∃y ∀x ((x ≠ y) → (M(x, y) ∧ ¬M(y, x))). Swapping to ∀y would describe everyone; ∃x would need only one other person.

truth-table-build.title: A truth table, column by column
truth-table-build.intro: The formula (p → q) ∧ (q → r) has three variables. We list all 8 assignments and add one column per sub-formula.

elements.text: Building the table of (p → q) ∧ (q → r), one column at a time
8 rows: p alternates slowest, T before F

steps.caption: Three variables give 2³ = 8 rows. The variable columns are filled first: p is T for the first four rows, q alternates in pairs, r every row.
Column p → q: it is false only where p = T and q = F, which is rows 3 and 4. Every other row keeps the promise.

set.text: p → q fails on rows 3 and 4

steps.caption: Column q → r: false only where q = T and r = F, rows 2 and 6.

set.text: q → r fails on rows 2 and 6

steps.caption: The conjunction is true only where both columns are T: rows 1, 5, 7 and 8 (TTT, FTT, FFT, FFF).
Read the true rows left to right: the values never drop from T to F along p, q, r. The column is the whole meaning of the formula.

set.text: true exactly when p, q, r never go T → F

unless-decoder.title: 'Unless' means 'if not'
unless-decoder.intro: The phrase 'unless Z' turns into the hypothesis 'not Z'. We decode a GATE sentence in three moves.

elements.text: Decoding “if X then Y unless Z”

elements.label: if X then Y  unless Z

steps.caption: Bracket the sentence first. 'Unless Z' qualifies the whole promise 'if X then Y'.
'A unless Z' means 'if not Z, then A'. With A = (X → Y) this is ¬Z → (X → Y).
Exportation moves the outer hypothesis inside: A → (B → C) ≡ (A ∧ B) → C. The result is (X ∧ ¬Z) → Y.
Check with the forbidden situation. The sentence is broken only if X happens, Z does not, and Y fails: X = T, Y = F, Z = F. The formula is false on exactly that row.

set.text: only forbidden row: X = T, Y = F, Z = F

verdict-columns.title: Tautology, contradiction, contingency
verdict-columns.intro: The verdict on a formula is read from its final column: all T, all F, or mixed. Three formulas in p and q, one of each kind.

steps.caption: Column A, q → (p → q): every row is T. A column of all T is a tautology (valid): true whatever p and q mean.
Column B, p ∧ ¬(p ∨ q): every row is F. ¬(p ∨ q) forces p = F, which clashes with the first conjunct. All F is a contradiction (unsatisfiable).
Column C, (p ∨ q) → q: false only on row 2 (p = T, q = F), true elsewhere. A mixed column is a contingency.
Satisfiable means at least one T: A and C are satisfiable, B is not. Falsifiable means at least one F: B and C. Only C is both.

set.text: satisfiable: A, C    falsifiable: B, C

steps.caption: Negating a formula flips its column: ¬A is all F, ¬B is all T, and ¬C is still mixed. Tautology and contradiction swap; contingency stays.
